The aggregate outlook is one in which EIBM will be required to continuously adjust to geopolitical changes, implement its most complex technological transformation to date and maintain operational effectiveness across all border domains. Sustained operational flexibility, accelerated interagency coordination and proactive contingency planning are the three most urgent management imperatives for the period ahead. Geopolitical shifts and the migratory flow Migratory pressure on the EU-Ukraine border is expected to remain manageable but structurally sensitive to developments related to the war and internal dynamics within Ukraine. In the absence of a major deterioration in the security environment, no sudden large-scale displacement from Ukraine towards the EU is anticipated over the next 12 months. However, the situation remains highly contingent on battlefield developments, mobilisation policies and domestic socioeconomic conditions. Overall, migration in South-Eastern Europe will continue to be affected by developments in traditional source regions, i.e. the Middle East and South-Central Asia, as well as by developments along the corridors via Libya. The US/Israeli war on Iran and relations between various groups and factions in Lebanon, Gaza and Syria remain key uncertainties which can still drive instability, ranging from localised skirmishes to potential regional conflicts. With the above caveats, absent a major regional destabilisation, and provided Türkiye continues to focus on preventing migratory spillovers, pressure on the Türkiye-EU corridors should be kept under control for the medium term. Still, given high geopolitical uncertainties, pressure upticks cannot be ruled out in the medium to long term. Unless Libyan prevention capabilities are significantly enhanced, pressure on this corridor is expected to remain high throughout 2026. Migration dynamics in the Western Balkans will continue to reflect, with some delay, developments in the Eastern Mediterranean and the key source and transit areas. Regional tensions in the Horn of Africa and the war in Sudan continue to act as major drivers of displacement, feeding longer-term migration pressure towards North Africa and Europe, with Libya remaining the principal transit and departure point for the Central Mediterranean route.

Migratory pressure on the Canary Islands is expected to remain moderate but changeable over the next 12 months, with episodic spikes, particularly during favourable weather. The main drivers of migratory pressure on this route are enforcement measures in the embarkation countries, regional instability in West Africa and the Sahel, and adaptive strategies by smuggling networks. While annual arrivals may remain below the exceptional levels of 2024, they could increase in relation to the lower levels observed in 2025 if enforcement measures weaken or smuggling networks successfully adapt to controls. The Western Mediterranean route is expected to see a steady flow of migrants, with a slight upward trend. The number of irregular migrants entering the EU by air in 2026 will likely be at levels similar to 2025. The number of irregular migrants of Latin American nationalities refused entry at EU airports will likely keep increasing in 2026. This is mostly due to measures introduced by the current US administration aimed at reducing irregular migration of Latin American nationals to the US. The number of asylum applications registered at the EU’s external air borders by Middle Eastern and Central Asian nationals may also increase. Migrants trying to enter the EU in an unauthorised manner could, where possible, abuse the Airport Transit Visa waiver to seek asylum in the EU. Others might use false or fraudulently obtained documents or present someone else's authentic passports as impostors to board flights to the EU. Future of hybrid threats In 2026, hybrid threats will present a multi-domain challenge with a sustained upward trajectory. Along the eastern borders, Russia and Belarus will highly likely intensify their hybrid operations with tactics ranging from instrumentalised migration, infrastructure sabotage and GPS jamming to the hostile use of drones and weather ballons and asymmetric pressure operations to test detection and reaction capabilities. The need to strengthen response capacities by the EBCG community has never been more pertinent. At air borders, state-sponsored instrumentalisation of migration and drone intrusions to disrupt air traffic will pose an elevated risk. On the southern and southernwestern borders, Russia’s expanding military footprint through the Africa Corps in the Sahel is weakening regional counterterrorism capacities, fuelling jihadist recruitment and positioning Moscow to potentially leverage migration flows as a geopolitical instrument against the EU, should it serve its political interest. The convergence of hybrid operations, organised criminal networks and regional instability is identified as one of the most consequential structural risks to the EU’s southern borders. Across all domains, the shared assessment is clear: throughout the forecast period, hybrid threats are expected to diversify in method, may expand in geography and will harden in intent to make prevention and detection an increasing challenge for EIBM. Operational risks The rollout of the EES and ETIAS will fundamentally reshape EU border management. Ensuring full operational preparedness is non-negotiable, encompassing thorough training for border personnel, expanded processing infrastructure at key crossing points, and refined passenger flow management protocols designed to minimise disruption and maximise throughput efficiency. Sustaining strategic agility is equally essential, enabling rapid policy adaptation in response to shifting geopolitical dynamics and emerging security threats.

for cocaine, Afghan heroin and cannabis. Trafficking of converted firearms from Türkiye represents a growing risk. Along the Western Mediterranean, narcolanchas carrying Moroccan cannabis will increasingly be used for transporting cocaine, as trafficking networks continue to restructure towards West African redistribution hubs, with semi-submersibles and fixed-wing drones representing the advancing technological frontier. Across all routes, the overriding challenge for EIBM will be the pace of adaptation by OCGs as they increasingly apply sophisticated, diversified distribution methods. In the maritime domain, particularly across the Mediterranean, organised crime will increasingly exploit commercial ships, fishing vessels and ports, using container flows and concealed compartments in vehicles to facilitate the transport of illicit goods. Frontex support for return activities EU-wide effective returns will continue their gradual upward trajectory, but the structural gap between the number of issued return decisions and the number of actual returns will persist, sustained by the sizeable return backlog, volatile timeline, as well as challenges such as limited cooperation on identification and documentation from countries of origin.

Cross-border crime Cross-border crime across all EU border regions will remain adaptive, profit-driven and technologically evolving rather than uniformly escalating. Migrant smuggling remains the overriding challenge for border management across all routes, as OCGs increasingly integrate sophisticated diversified methods to counter enforcement efforts. Along the eastern borders, cigarette and excise goods smuggling will remain the most persistent threat. Weapons trafficking is assessed as a high-impact but moderate-likelihood risk, unlikely to materialise unless the war in Ukraine de-escalates to the point of demobilisation of combatants and arms surpluses. Detections of stolen vehicles, document fraud and dualuse goods smuggling are expected to grow. In the Western Balkans, OCGs will ensure the region maintains its status as the primary EU transit corridor

The Agency’s support for return operations has grown substantially in recent years, from 7 952 (11% of all effective returns) in 2020 to around 63 500 in 2025 (42% of all effective returns), and Frontex is expected to remain a key partner for Member States in the years to come. The implementation of the EU Pact on Migration and Asylum as of June 2026 is expected to have a considerable impact on the total numbers of returns. However, the first results of the Pact will only be visible at the end of 2026, and the long-term effects will need to be measured in perspective of the overall migratory situational picture. Legislative reforms on return regulation, return digitalisation and changes to Frontex’s mandate are expected to lead to changes in overall EU returns as well as Frontex’s role in the next two years.

Secondary movements within the EU/Schengen area are structurally embedded in the EU’s migration system and are projected to persist through 2026 and 2027. Even if irregular arrivals at external borders level off or moderately decrease, movements within the Schengen area will likely persist, as they are primarily driven by different socioeconomic opportunities, as well differences in asylum procedures, reception conditions and return effectiveness in particular Member States. Policy reforms and enforcement measures may shape the scale and direction of these internal flows, but they will not fundamentally remove the underlying incentives.

The coming months will be decisive for the future of Schengen and the EU’s migration framework. Success hinges on three key actions: accelerating operational readiness for the Pact, with a focus on screening capabilities and reception capacity; strengthening Frontex’s role through mandate expansion and increased resourcing; and fostering political alignment to prevent the permanent normalisation of internal border controls, which would deal a severe blow to European integration.

The EU Pact on Migration and Asylum is anticipated to yield procedural harmonisation over the medium to long term; however, its near-term effect on secondary movement reduction will be negligible, particularly within the 2026 timeframe. Geographically, the Western Balkan corridor – traversing Serbia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Croatia toward Slovenia and Austria – is likely to remain the dominant transit pathway for secondary flows originating from the Eastern Mediterranean, with intensity subject to variations based on enforcement measures. Secondary movements linked to the Central Mediterranean and Western African/Western Mediterranean routes are directly correlated with arrival volumes in frontline Member States, given the high onward movement rate among those entering via these corridors. Consequently, fluctuations along these routes have a cascading effect on secondary movement distribution across the Schengen area. Finally, the national composition of secondary movement flows is mainly mirroring the nationality profile of external border crossings, with the most frequently detected irregularly crossing nationalities accounting for the majority of internal detections.

The June deadline for the implementation of the EU Pact on Migration and Asylum is not just a technical milestone; it is a test of Europe’s ability to unite behind a common approach to migration. Failure to deliver a functional, fair and sustainable system risks deepening divisions. On the other hand, success would reaffirm the EU’s capacity to act collectively in the face of shared challenges, as reflected by the ‘New border IT: the transformation that comes with commensurate risks’ section of the executive summary. The choices made today will shape Europe’s security, cohesion and global standing for years to come. Forward planning To confront the accelerating complexity of the geopolitical environment, hybrid threats, cross-border crime, and the transformation of the EU’s migration and asylum system, the EU must embrace a proactive and adaptive approach, anchored in predictive EIBM intelligence and a flexible operational response. This will enable the EU and its Member States to navigate a risk landscape dense with structural challenges and serious threats to the security of the external borders. A predictive approach must be built on access to comprehensive data sets, the complete operationalisation of EUROSUR functionalities, and robust mechanisms for processing and disseminating intelligence across a broad range of institutional actors and professional communities.

Strengthening border resilience must be treated as a strategic priority, requiring sustained investment in advanced surveillance technology, intelligencesharing frameworks and targeted capacity-building programmes. Frontex understands that discussions are ongoing as to a possible supportive role of the Agency on the security of border infrastructure and in the development of countermeasures against hybrid operations targeting them. In the domain of cooperation with third countries, deepening multilateral partnerships with North African and Western Balkan counterparts will be indispensable in dismantling the organised criminal networks involved in people smuggling and other cross-border crime. The EU must reinforce its return architecture by better balancing the growing operational role of Frontex with robust and accountable national capabilities. This balanced approach will ensure that return operations remain effective, legally sound and consistent with humanitarian obligations. By aligning operational readiness with long-term strategic foresight, the EU will be significantly better positioned to safeguard its borders while upholding its foundational commitments to security, human rights and regional stability. Strategic Risk Analysis 2026: essential reading for a longer-term perspective Looking beyond the year ahead, Frontex’s Strategic Risk Analysis 2026, which is to be published in the second half of the year, will have a 10-year time horizon with scenarios for European Border Management up to 2036. The report will focus on megatrends, such as increasing demographic imbalances, accelerating technological change, hyperconnectivity and widening inequalities – to name a few – and will analyse the areas most relevant for border management. The report is designed to enable strategic, legislative and operational decisions to be taken to enhance border management in the longer term.
